To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the development of integrated water models is challenging due to existing knowledge gaps and data limitations.

the future of integrated water quality modeling will depend on: (1) improved knowledge of biogeochemical process dynamics at different scales and (2) development of advanced uncertainty analysis techniques.

‘The future of water quality modelling will be characterized by a shift towards the development of integrated process‐oriented models that effectively couple the catchment and receiving waterbody processes and that are capable of handling the ‘change of scale’ problem’.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of integrated water‐quality models that are able to predict the fate and transport of nutrients in river systems.

the development of a process‐based integrated water quality model that is able to predict water quality at multiple scales, to account for spatial and temporal variability in catchments and in‐stream systems, and to quantify the uncertainties associated with parameter estimation, measurement errors and model structure.

the development of integrated water‐quality models and the application of these models in the context of water quality monitoring and assessment, water quality management, and water resources management.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
integrated water quality modelling has reached a certain degree of maturity, but there are still many challenges ahead.
integrated water quality models are not ready to be used for the management of water quality problems, but that they have the potential to be useful in the future.

the future of water quality modelling will be characterized by the need of more and better data to improve the parameterization of the model, the need to better represent processes and their interactions, the need to improve the model structure and its parameter estimation, and the need for more and better model applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we need a new generation of integrated water quality and nutrient modelling tools that are capable of addressing current challenges and future needs.

we need to improve our understanding of landscape biogeochemical and in‐stream processes, we need to better understand how these processes scale, we need to develop novel uncertainty analysis techniques, and we need to better articulate the coupling between catchment and in stream models.
we are not able to predict the future, but we are able to predict what we can do to influence the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the development of next‐generation integrated water quality models requires the adoption of a more comprehensive and systematic approach that will facilitate the identification of research needs, the articulation of process knowledge, and the development of novel model calibration techniques.

the development of integrated water models that are more reliable, more accurate, and more robust is possible only by means of a concerted effort from the modelling, field and remote sensing communities.
the development of next‐generation models requires the integration of new process knowledge and novel model calibration techniques.
